pages.title: Contribution or exchange?
pages.question: Is this incoming money a gift (ASC 958-605) or payment for something (ASC 606 or other guidance)?
pages.summary: Money that comes in is either a gift (a contribution) or payment for something the payer gets back (an exchange). It is an exchange only when the payer itself receives roughly equal value. Benefit to the public, to the funder's mission, or the good feeling of giving does not count as value received.
askYourPro: Does anything in this grant or contract give the funder goods or services of roughly equal value in return?
Is this a third-party payer arrangement (Medicaid, insurance, vouchers) that should be treated as exchange revenue?
How should we split payments that are part gift and part purchase, and where does each part go on Form 990 Part VIII?

steps.text: Does the payer itself receive goods or services of roughly equal value?
sub: Yes: treat it as an exchange (ASC 606 or other revenue guidance).
No: go to the next question.

steps.text: Is the payer paying on behalf of an identified customer who receives the goods or services (for example Medicaid, insurance, or a tuition voucher)?
sub: Yes: treat it as an exchange with a third-party payer.
No: it is a contribution. Next, decide whether it is conditional.

pages.html:
The rule in one line

It is an exchange only if the party paying receives value of roughly equal worth in return. Benefit to the public, or to the payer's mission, does not count as value received.

What does NOT count as value to the payer

ASU 2018-08 settled these, and they decide most grant questions:

  • Public benefit. A foundation or government agency is not the same as the public. When the public benefits from what the money pays for, the funder has not received that value.
  • Mission fulfillment. Advancing the funder's own mission is not value received.
  • Good feeling. The donor's satisfaction from giving is not value received.

Indicators in the current standard (958-605-15-5A, as rewritten by ASU 2018-08)

ASU 2018-08 replaced the older, longer indicator list. What the standard now says:

Points toward exchange Points toward contribution
Contract penalties for nonperformance go beyond returning the money transferred The funder had full discretion over the amount; it wasn't set by the value of a deliverable
The type of funder (foundation, government, corporation) doesn't matter on its own

Plus the three "not value to the payer" rules above.

Practice judgment (not in the current standard; use as supporting evidence only)

  • Both parties described the deal as a purchase of goods or services at a negotiated price.
  • The payer owns or directly uses the work product.
  • The recipient solicited the money without offering anything of equal value back.

Older guides and audit memos still cite these from the pre-2018 indicator table. They can support a conclusion, but don't rest a memo on them alone.

Common cases

Situation Usual answer Why
Foundation program grant with reporting requirements Contribution Reporting is not value to the foundation; the public is the beneficiary
Government grant to run a public program Contribution (often conditional) Same reasoning; check for barriers next
Government contract to deliver services to the agency itself Exchange The agency receives the services
Medicaid or insurance reimbursement for client services Exchange Third-party payer on behalf of an identified customer
Sponsor payment with tickets, ads, or exclusive rights Split: exchange for the benefits, contribution for the rest See Corporate sponsorships
Gala ticket Split: exchange for the meal and event, contribution for the rest See Quid pro quo gifts, events, and acknowledgments
Membership dues with real member benefits Split, or exchange if benefits roughly equal the dues Value the benefits

Coding notes

  • Exchange revenue goes in program service revenue, fees, or contract revenue lines, not contribution lines. That choice also drives Form 990 Part VIII (contributions on line 1, program service revenue on line 2).
  • When you split a payment, record the two pieces separately at the time of receipt. Reconstructing the split at year-end is where errors come from.
  • Write down which indicators drove the call. When the auditor asks, the memo is the evidence.

pages.title: Conditional or unconditional?
pages.question: When do I record a contribution as revenue?
pages.summary: A contribution is conditional only when the agreement has both a barrier the organization must clear and a right for the donor to take the money back (or not pay) if the barrier is not cleared. If either piece is missing, the gift is recorded when it is received or promised.
askYourPro: Does this grant agreement contain a measurable barrier, and does the funder have a right of return or release?
Should cash we received in advance on this grant sit in a refundable advance (liability) until the barrier is met?
Which parts of this agreement are conditional and which are unconditional?

steps.text: Is there a barrier the organization must overcome to be entitled to the money?
sub: No: the contribution is unconditional. Record it now, then check for donor restrictions.
Yes: go to the next question.

steps.text: Does the donor have a right of return, or a right to be released from paying, if the barrier is not met?
sub: No: the contribution is unconditional.
Yes: the contribution is conditional. Record no revenue yet; cash received is a refundable advance.

steps: When the barrier is substantially met, the contribution becomes unconditional and is recorded as revenue.

pages.html:
The rule in one line

A contribution is conditional only when the agreement has both a barrier the organization must overcome and a right for the donor to get the money back (or to be released from paying) if the barrier isn't met. If either piece is missing, it's unconditional and is recorded when received or promised.

Indicators of a barrier (weigh together; none is decisive)

  1. A measurable, performance-related target. Examples: serve 500 households, raise a matching amount, hold a specified number of sessions.
  2. Limited discretion over how the activity is carried out. Example: the agreement dictates staffing qualifications or protocols in detail.
  3. The stipulation is tied to the purpose of the agreement. Administrative requirements such as routine reporting usually are not barriers.

Common cases

Agreement language Barrier? Return or release? Result
"Grant of $100,000 to be paid as costs are incurred; unspent funds revert" Yes: incurring qualifying costs Yes Conditional; recognize as costs are incurred
"$50,000 if you raise $50,000 in matching gifts by June 30" Yes: the match Yes: no payment if unmet Conditional until the match is raised
"$25,000 for the literacy program; submit an annual report" No: the report is administrative Doesn't matter Unconditional, purpose-restricted
"$10,000; return any amount not used for the program" No measurable barrier Yes Unconditional, restricted. A right of return alone does not make it conditional
Multi-year pledge with no conditions No No Unconditional; implied time restriction (see With or without donor restrictions?)

Coding notes

  • Cash received on a conditional grant goes to a refundable advance (liability), not revenue.
  • Conditional promises not yet received are not recorded at all; they are disclosed in the notes.
  • Partly conditional agreements are common: recognize the unconditional piece now and the conditional piece as each barrier is met.
  • If an agreement is ambiguous about whether a stipulation is a barrier, the standard presumes the contribution is conditional (958-605-25-5E).
  • How likely the organization is to meet the barrier doesn't matter. A barrier you will certainly clear is still a barrier (958-605-25-5C).
  • Federal cost-reimbursement grants are the classic conditional contribution. They are not exchanges just because they come from government.

pages.summary: Only a donor can restrict a gift, by limiting it to a purpose or time period narrower than the organization's mission. Board-designated money stays "without donor restrictions." Restricted amounts are released when the purpose is met or the time passes.

sub: No, and it is not a promise payable in a future period: without donor restrictions.
No, but it is a promise payable in a future period: with donor restrictions (implied time restriction).

pages.html:
The rule in one line

Only a donor can restrict a gift. A restriction exists when the donor limits the gift to a purpose or a time period more specific than the organization's general mission. The board can earmark unrestricted money, but that remains "without donor restrictions" (board-designated).

Tests for whether the donor actually restricted it

  • Source documents decide. Gift agreement, response card, appeal language, online form designation, email from the donor. Keep it with the gift record.
  • Appeal language counts. If the appeal said "give to the new van fund," gifts responding to it are purpose-restricted even if the donor wrote nothing.
  • Mission-level purpose is not a restriction. "For your programs" or "to support your work" at an org that only does that work is unrestricted.
  • Board action never creates a donor restriction. Board-designated funds (operating reserve, quasi-endowment) stay without donor restrictions and are disclosed by amount and purpose.

Release mechanics

Restriction type Released when
Purpose Qualifying expenses are incurred
Time (explicit date) The date passes
Time (implied, pledge payments) The payment is due / received in the period it was meant for
Long-lived asset purchase The asset is placed in service (unless the donor stipulated a longer restriction)
Perpetual (endowment corpus) Never; earnings follow the gift instrument and state UPMIFA law

Same-period policy option

An organization can elect to report restricted gifts whose restriction is met in the same reporting period as "without donor restrictions," provided it treats investment gains the same way, applies the policy consistently, and discloses it (958-605-45-4A). ASU 2018-08 added a separate version of this election limited to gifts that started out conditional (958-605-45-4B). Note which policy, if any, each client has elected in their client file; it changes how you code every restricted gift.

Coding notes

  • Use a fund or class dimension in the GL for each restriction, not separate revenue accounts per fund. Revenue accounts describe the type of income; the fund dimension describes the restriction.
  • Release entries are reclassifications between net asset classes, not revenue.
  • A gift with both purpose and time restrictions is released only when both are satisfied.
  • The CRM's "designation" field and the GL's restriction are not automatically the same thing. A CRM designation can be the donor's soft preference. Map designations to restriction status explicitly (see GAAP vs. fundraising counting).

pages.html:
The rule in one line

Record donated goods, use of facilities, and qualifying services at fair value when received, show them on their own line apart from cash gifts, and disclose them by category. Exception: contributed collection items (art, historical treasures) that meet the collections criteria in 958-605-25-19 need not be recognized; that matters for museums and historical societies. The IRS side (Forms 8283 and 8282, Schedule M) runs on separate thresholds.

Valuation

  • Use fair value at the date of the gift. The organization values the gift for its books; that is independent of what the donor claims.
  • The organization should not state a dollar value on the donor's acknowledgment for noncash gifts. Describe the item; valuation is the donor's job (see Pub. 1771 and Pub. 561).
  • A donor's appraisal can inform your fair value but doesn't bind you.
  • Document the valuation technique and inputs; ASU 2020-07 requires disclosing them.

Disclosure checklist (ASU 2020-07)

For each category of contributed nonfinancial assets recognized:

  • Amount, by category (e.g., food, supplies, professional services, facilities)
  • Whether the items were used or sold during the period; for items used, which programs or activities used them
  • The organization's policy, if any, on selling rather than using donated items
  • Any donor restrictions attached
  • Valuation techniques and inputs, and the principal market used if the organization is barred from selling or using the item there

IRS paperwork that follows the gift

Trigger Requirement Row in volatile-values.md
Donor's noncash gift over $5,000 Org signs Form 8283 Section B (acknowledging receipt, not value) form-8283-b
Org sells or disposes of that property within 3 years of receiving it File Form 8282 within 125 days; send the donor a copy. Not required for items the donor certified at $500 or less, or items consumed or distributed for charitable purposes form-8282
Aggregate noncash gifts above the threshold, or any art, historical treasures, or conservation contributions File Schedule M with Form 990 sched-m
Noncash gift of $250+ Written acknowledgment describing the property (no value) cwa-threshold

Coding notes

  • Use separate revenue accounts for contributed nonfinancial assets so the statement of activities line comes straight from the GL.
  • Offset to the matching expense (if consumed) or asset (if held) at the same fair value.
  • Keep a disposal log for items received with a signed Form 8283 Section B; the 3-year clock is easy to miss.
  • Services from an affiliate's personnel that directly benefit the organization follow a separate rule; ask your accountant if an affiliated organization lends you staff.
  • Volunteer hours that don't meet the services test can still appear in narrative reporting and grant match documentation; they just don't hit the GL.

pages.html:
The rule in one line

When a donor gets something back, only the amount above the fair market value of what they received is a gift. If the payment is over $75, the charity must tell the donor that in writing, unless the benefit is small enough to ignore under the IRS safe harbors.

Safe harbors for ignoring a benefit

Use the current year's figures in Key numbers (rows low-cost-article, token-min-payment, two-percent-cap, membership-exception).

Both of the first two safe harbors only apply when the payment is made as part of a fundraising campaign and the charity tells the donor how much of the payment is deductible (Pub. 1771, PDF p. 6; Rev. Proc. 90-12 sec. 3). Without that statement, value the benefit.

  1. Token items. The donor pays at least the minimum, receives only items bearing the org's name or logo (mug, calendar, tote), and the org's total cost for those items is within the low-cost article ceiling. Measured by the charity's cost, not the item's retail value.
  2. 2% test. The fair market value of everything the donor receives is no more than 2% of the payment and no more than the annual dollar cap.
  3. Free, unordered items mailed with a solicitation fall within the low-cost article rules (Rev. Proc. 92-49).
  4. Membership-benefits exception. An annual payment of $75 or less that buys only recurring member privileges (free or discounted admission, gift-shop or parking discounts, member-only events within the low-cost limits) is treated as insubstantial. Membership dues at that level don't need to be split (Pub. 1771, PDF p. 6).

Rev. Proc. 90-12 states that benefits in cash or cash equivalents are never insubstantial (text read via the Tax Notes reproduction; not yet checked against the IRS copy). Treat gift cards as valued benefits.

What the $250+ acknowledgment must say (Pub. 1771, PDF pp. 3-5)

  • Name of the organization and the amount of cash, or a description (not the value) of noncash property.
  • A statement of whether the organization provided any goods or services in return. This is the element receipts most often miss. "No goods or services were provided" is enough when true.
  • If goods or services were provided: a description and good-faith estimate of their value, or a statement that only intangible religious benefits were provided.
  • It must reach the donor by the earlier of the date they file their return or the return's due date (with extensions).

What the written disclosure must say (payments over $75)

  • The deductible amount is limited to what the donor paid in excess of the value of the goods or services received.
  • A good-faith estimate of that value.
  • It can be combined with the $250 acknowledgment in one letter.

Event coding

Item Treatment
Gala ticket Split at the ticket's fair value of the benefits (meal, entertainment): exchange revenue for the benefit, contribution for the rest
Auction item purchase Buyer's payment above the item's fair value is a contribution; up to fair value is exchange revenue. Donated auction item is an in-kind gift recorded when received
Sponsorship of the event See Corporate sponsorships
Raffle ticket Not a contribution at all; gaming rules apply
Donor declines the benefit at purchase If declined in advance and the org documents it, the full amount can be a gift. Not attending, without declining, doesn't count

Fair value is what the benefit would cost in a normal market (a comparable dinner at a comparable venue), not what the org paid. A donated venue doesn't make the dinner worth $0.

Coding notes

  • Book the exchange and contribution portions to separate accounts at receipt. Most CRMs support a "non-deductible" or "benefit value" field on the gift; map it to the exchange account in the GL integration.
  • On Form 990, the contribution portion of event payments goes on Part VIII line 1c (and is shown again in parentheses on line 8a); the exchange portion goes on line 8a, with direct benefit costs on line 8b. Keep event expenses tagged to the event; indirect fundraising costs go in Part IX column (D), not line 8b. If donors receive only items of nominal value, the whole amount is reported as contributions and nothing goes on line 8 (Instructions for Form 990, TY2025, PDF pp. 38 and 41).
  • Keep the fair-value estimate memo for each event with the event's records.

pages.html:
Sponsorships need two separate answers: one for the IRS (is any of this taxable unrelated business income?) and one for GAAP (how much is contribution vs. exchange revenue?). They usually line up, but they are different tests.

The rule in one line

A business can be thanked by name and logo without the payment becoming taxable. Once the business receives advertising, exclusivity as a provider, or other benefits worth more than 2% of the payment, the value of those benefits stops being a qualified sponsorship payment.

Acknowledgment vs. advertising

Allowed (acknowledgment) Turns it into advertising
Sponsor name, logo, slogan that doesn't compare or praise Qualitative or comparative descriptions ("the best coffee in town")
Address, phone, website Price information or discounts
Value-neutral list of product lines Endorsements
Display or distribution of the sponsor's products at the event Inducements to buy, sell, or use the products
Exclusive sponsor of the event Exclusive provider arrangement (only their product may be sold or used)

Two things are never qualified sponsorship payments, whatever the sponsor receives:

  • Contingent payments. A payment whose amount depends on attendance, broadcast ratings, or other measures of public exposure. (A payment can depend on the event actually happening.)
  • Periodical ads and trade shows. Payments for ads in the organization's magazines or newsletters, and qualified convention or trade-show activity, fall under other rules.

A payment that is not a qualified sponsorship payment is not automatically taxable. It is unrelated business income only if the activity is a regularly carried on trade or business; a one-time event often isn't. Run that question with the tax preparer.

GAAP side

  • Benefits with real value (tickets, tables, booth space, hospitality, advertising): that portion is an exchange, recognized under ASC 606 when the benefit is delivered.
  • The remainder is a contribution, and may be restricted if the sponsor tied it to a specific program.
  • Acknowledgment alone (name and logo) is generally not treated as commensurate value, so a pure name-and-logo sponsorship is usually entirely a contribution.

Sponsorship packet checklist

  • List every benefit in each sponsorship tier with an estimated fair value
  • Check each tier's benefits against the 2% test
  • Review the sponsor-facing copy for advertising language before it's printed
  • Confirm no exclusive-provider language in the agreement unless the tax preparer has signed off
  • Record the exchange and contribution portions separately at receipt

pages.html:
The rule in one line

GAAP answers "what does the organization have a right to, and when?" Fundraising counting answers "what did fundraisers secure, and who gets credit?" Both are legitimate; they just measure different things. Every CRM field and every report should state which rule it follows.

Where the two diverge

Item GAAP (ledger) Fundraising counting (CRM, campaign reports)
Unconditional multi-year pledge Full amount recognized when promised, discounted to present value, less an allowance Counted at face value when documented. CASE's 2024 update removed the five-year cap, so New Funds Committed now includes the full documented pledge
Conditional pledge or grant Not recognized until barriers are met Often counted when committed, depending on the organization's counting policy
Revocable bequest intention Not recognized CASE counts documented bequest intentions in New Funds Committed; they reach Funds Received only when realized
Irrevocable deferred gifts (e.g., charitable remainder trusts) Recognized under split-interest guidance at present value Counted under specific CASE rules, often at face and present value
Soft credits (spouse, DAF advisor, board member who solicited) Not a concept; one donor of record Credit to multiple people for recognition and reporting
Gala ticket Split into exchange and contribution Often counted in full as "event revenue raised"
Matching gift from an employer Contribution from the employer Often soft-credited to the employee
In-kind gifts Recognized at fair value per the in-kind rules Counting policies vary; many organizations exclude them from cash goals

How to keep both straight in a system

  1. Two fields, not one. Keep "GAAP amount" and "counting amount" separate on the gift record, or derive one from the other with documented rules. Never let a report silently mix them.
  2. Name the rule on every report. "Raised (CASE counting)" and "Contribution revenue (GAAP)" are different report titles, and both are defensible.
  3. Reconcile monthly. A one-page reconciliation from CRM "raised" to GL contribution revenue, by reason code (pledge timing, conditional, soft credit, benefit value, in-kind), catches coding errors early and is the document auditors ask for.
  4. Write a counting policy. If the organization has no written counting policy, borrow CASE's as the starting point and note where you depart from it.
  5. Designation is not restriction. A CRM designation can be a soft preference. Map each designation to a GAAP restriction status explicitly (see With or without donor restrictions?).

Single Audit threshold $1,000,000 in federal expenditures (was $750,000) 2 CFR 200.501 S

Several institutions report applying the new equipment and MTDC thresholds only once their negotiated rate agreement is renewed. Check the award terms and the client's rate agreement before assuming the new numbers apply.

  • Repo created: sources.yaml (24 sources), volatile-values.md (2025 and 2026 columns), seven decision files, quarterly watcher with 15 offline tests.
  • Verification status at creation: 8 primary, 11 secondary, 5 pending sources.

Proc. 2025-32 sec. 4.33 (2026 token amounts), Pub. 1771 (Rev. 11-2023), Form 990 instructions (TY2025), Schedule M instructions (TY2025), Form 8282 instructions (Rev. October 2021), Pub. 561 (Rev. December 2025), Pub. 598 (Rev. March 2021), Pub. 4221-PC (Rev. 3-2018).
  • Baseline watcher run from the build environment. FASB, CASE, and the legacy UCOA URL refused automated requests (403) there; the first GitHub Actions run will show whether they also refuse GitHub. If they do, they stay on the "check by hand" list each quarter.
  • Wayback captures could not be made from the build environment; the watcher retries them automatically on the next run.
  • Independent fact-check (separate reviewer, same day) corrected: the Form 8282 three-year clock (runs from receipt, not from signing Form 8283) and its exceptions; the campaign-and-disclosure condition on the token and 2% safe harbors; the missing membership-benefits exception and $250 acknowledgment contents; Treas. Reg. 1.513-4 paragraph numbers; the contribution-vs-exchange indicator table (pre-2018 indicators moved to "practice judgment"); CASE bequest and multi-year pledge counting; 2025 tax-law carryforward and exclusions. Resolved paragraph numbers: 958-605-25-5E, 25-5C, 45-4A, 45-4B, 15-6(e), 25-19.
  • Open verification backlog:
    • Read the ASC paragraphs cited as secondary in Basic View and upgrade them (FASB login required).
    • Confirm ASC 958-605-25-16 (contributed services criteria).
    • Confirm Rev. Proc. 90-12's cash-equivalent statement against the IRS copy.
    • Confirm the current home of the UCOA and the FASB ASU index URL.
    • Read the CASE Global Reporting Standards (current edition) before citing specific counting rules in client policy.
